subject: Science
status: DRAFT — for review by a Science teacher before it is relied on
source: Drafted against the NCERT Class X Science textbook (jesc1, 2025-26 rationalised reprint) and the 410 questions imported from C:/dev/sirah_project/NCERT/data. Content CBSE removed in 2023 — Evolution in Heredity, electromagnetic induction and the electric generator in Magnetic Effects, sources of energy, and management of natural resources — is deliberately absent.
notes: The imported bank still holds questions labelled '[Out of syllabus: Evolution ...]' in Chapter 8 and '[Out of syllabus: AC and DC generators ...]' in Chapter 12. No outcome here covers them, on purpose: linking them would make removed content count towards a student's mastery.

outcomes.statement: Writes a word equation and a skeletal chemical equation for a described reaction, including the state symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq).
Balances a chemical equation by the hit-and-trial method and explains why the law of conservation of mass requires it.
Classifies a given reaction as combination, decomposition, displacement or double displacement, and justifies the classification from the equation.
Distinguishes exothermic from endothermic reactions, and identifies thermal, electrolytic and photolytic decomposition in examples.
Identifies the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in a redox reaction, in terms of gain or loss of oxygen or hydrogen.
Explains corrosion and rancidity as effects of oxidation in everyday life, and describes how each is prevented.

topics.title: Chemical properties of acids and bases

outcomes.statement: Identifies acids and bases using indicators such as litmus, phenolphthalein, methyl orange and olfactory indicators.
Predicts the products when an acid reacts with a metal, a metal carbonate, a metal hydrogencarbonate or a metal oxide, and when a base reacts with an acid.
Explains that acids produce H⁺(aq) ions and bases produce OH⁻(aq) ions in water, and why diluting an acid must be done by adding acid to water.

topics.title: Strength of acids and bases, and salts

outcomes.statement: Interprets the pH scale to judge whether a solution is acidic, neutral or basic and how strong it is, and relates pH to digestion, tooth decay and soil.
Describes the preparation and uses of sodium hydroxide by the chlor-alkali process, bleaching powder, baking soda, washing soda and plaster of Paris.
Explains water of crystallisation using copper sulphate and gypsum, and identifies which common salts contain it.
Compares metals and non-metals by lustre, malleability, ductility, conductivity and sonority, and names the exceptions to each property.
Describes how metals react with oxygen, water and dilute acids, and identifies amphoteric oxides.
Uses the reactivity series to predict whether one metal will displace another from a solution of its salt.
Explains the formation of an ionic compound by transfer of electrons, and relates it to the properties of ionic compounds.
Describes the steps in extracting a metal of low, medium or high reactivity, including roasting, calcination and reduction.
Explains electrolytic refining of a metal, identifying what happens at the anode and the cathode.
Explains how corrosion of metals is prevented by painting, galvanising and alloying.

concepts.name: Reactivity of metals and ionic compounds

outcomes.statement: Explains covalent bonding in carbon compounds, and draws electron-dot structures of molecules such as methane, ammonia and oxygen.
Describes the allotropes of carbon — diamond, graphite and fullerene — and relates their structures to their properties.
Identifies saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons, homologous series and structural isomers.
Names carbon compounds containing a functional group such as a halogen, alcohol, aldehyde, ketone or carboxylic acid.

topics.title: Chemical properties and important carbon compounds

outcomes.statement: Describes combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions of carbon compounds, with an example of each.
Describes the properties and reactions of ethanol and ethanoic acid, including esterification and saponification.
Explains how soap removes oil by forming micelles, and why soap works poorly in hard water where detergents do not.

concepts.name: Covalent bonding and structure of carbon compounds

outcomes.statement: Explains photosynthesis — the raw materials, the role of chlorophyll and stomata, and the products.
Describes digestion in the human alimentary canal, naming the organs in order and the role of each digestive juice.
Compares aerobic and anaerobic respiration, including the breakdown of glucose in yeast and in muscle cells.
Describes the human respiratory system and how exchange of gases takes place in the alveoli.
Describes double circulation through the four-chambered heart and the roles of arteries, veins, capillaries and valves.
Explains transport of water through xylem and of food through phloem in plants, including transpiration.
Describes how the nephron filters blood and forms urine, and names the path of urine out of the body.
Describes the structure of a neuron and how a nerve impulse travels from dendrite to axon and across a synapse.
Explains a reflex action by tracing its reflex arc, and distinguishes voluntary, involuntary and reflex actions.
Identifies the parts of the human brain and the function of each, and how the brain and spinal cord are protected.

topics.title: Coordination in plants and hormones in animals

outcomes.statement: Distinguishes the responses of plants to stimuli — phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism and chemotropism — and immediate movements such as in the sensitive plant.
Names the plant hormones auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin and abscisic acid, and states the effect of each.
Relates each human endocrine gland to the hormone it secretes and its function, and explains feedback control of hormone levels.

concepts.name: Hormonal coordination in plants and animals

topics.title: Modes of reproduction in single organisms

outcomes.statement: Explains why DNA copying during reproduction produces both similarity and variation, and why variation matters to a species.
Describes asexual reproduction by fission, fragmentation, regeneration, budding, spore formation and vegetative propagation, with an example of each.
Describes the parts of a flower and the sequence of pollination, fertilisation and seed formation.
Describes the human male and female reproductive systems and the path of sperm and ovum up to implantation.
Explains the changes at puberty, methods of contraception and how sexually transmitted diseases spread.

concepts.name: Sexual reproduction in plants and humans

outcomes.statement: Explains how variation accumulates across generations during reproduction.
Predicts the traits and ratios in the F1 and F2 generations of Mendel's monohybrid and dihybrid crosses.
Distinguishes dominant from recessive traits and genotype from phenotype, and explains how genes control a trait through proteins.
Explains sex determination in humans, and why the father's chromosome decides the sex of the child.
States the laws of reflection and describes the image formed by a plane mirror.
Draws ray diagrams for concave and convex mirrors and describes the position, nature and size of the image for each object position.
Applies the mirror formula and magnification with the New Cartesian sign convention to find an unknown distance or image size.
Explains refraction through a rectangular glass slab and relates refractive index to the speed of light in two media.
Draws ray diagrams for convex and concave lenses and describes the image for each object position.
Applies the lens formula, magnification and power of a lens in dioptres to solve numerical problems.

topics.title: The human eye and its defects

outcomes.statement: Describes the parts of the human eye and explains accommodation and the least distance of distinct vision.
Explains myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia, and identifies the lens that corrects each.

topics.title: Refraction through a prism and scattering

outcomes.statement: Explains dispersion of white light by a glass prism and the formation of a rainbow.
Explains effects of atmospheric refraction such as twinkling stars and early sunrise.
Explains scattering of light, the Tyndall effect, the blue colour of the sky and the reddening of the Sun at sunrise and sunset.

concepts.name: Defects of vision and their correction

topics.title: Current, potential difference and Ohm's law

outcomes.statement: Defines electric current, charge and potential difference with their SI units, and calculates charge or number of electrons from current and time.
Applies Ohm's law to relate potential difference, current and resistance in a circuit.
Explains how the resistance of a conductor depends on its length, area of cross-section and material, and uses resistivity in calculations.

topics.title: Combinations of resistors and the heating effect

outcomes.statement: Calculates the equivalent resistance of resistors in series and in parallel, and the current and voltage in each.
Applies Joule's law of heating and describes practical uses of the heating effect of current.
Calculates electric power and energy consumed in kilowatt-hours, and relates P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

concepts.name: Resistors in circuits and electric power

topics.title: Magnetic field due to a current

outcomes.statement: Describes magnetic field lines and their properties, including what closely spaced lines indicate.
Describes the magnetic field around a straight conductor, a circular loop and a solenoid, and applies the right-hand thumb rule.
Explains how an electromagnet is made and how its strength can be increased.

topics.title: Force on a conductor and domestic circuits

outcomes.statement: Applies Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
Describes domestic electric circuits — live, neutral and earth wires, fuses, and separate 5 A and 15 A circuits — and why each safety feature is used.

concepts.name: Force on a current and domestic circuits

outcomes.statement: Identifies the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem and classifies organisms as producers, consumers and decomposers.
Constructs food chains and food webs and identifies the trophic level of each organism.
Applies the ten per cent law to calculate energy available at a trophic level, and explains biological magnification.

topics.title: How our activities affect the environment

outcomes.statement: Explains how ozone forms in the upper atmosphere, why it matters, and how CFCs deplete it.
Classifies waste as biodegradable or non-biodegradable and evaluates ways of managing garbage.

prerequisites.requires: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
prerequisites.why: Valency decides every formula you will write this year, and valency comes from where the electrons sit.
pH and dilution are statements about concentration, which is the Class 9 solutions chapter.

prerequisites.concept: Reactivity of metals and ionic compounds
prerequisites.why: Ionic bonding — a metal handing electrons to a non-metal — is the single idea that explains how metals behave.

prerequisites.concept: Covalent bonding and structure of carbon compounds
prerequisites.why: Every structure you draw this chapter is a covalent bond diagram, which Class 9 already taught.
Nutrition, respiration and transport happen inside a cell before they happen inside you.
A reflex arc is nervous tissue wired to muscular tissue. Both were named and drawn in Class 9.

prerequisites.concept: Resistors in circuits and electric power
prerequisites.why: Electrical energy and power are the same work-and-power definitions from Class 9, with charge doing the moving.
